questions.stem: Which statement expresses the first law of thermodynamics, as it applies to Earth systems?
options: Energy is created whenever sunlight is absorbed by Earth's surface
Energy always flows from cold objects to hotter objects when in contact
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or transformed
Energy is always destroyed when it changes from one form to another
questions.explanation: The first law is the law of conservation of energy: the total energy of an isolated system stays constant, though it can change form or move between places. Heat flowing from hot to cold is described by the second law.

questions.stem: Over many years, the energy Earth absorbs from the Sun is roughly balanced by the energy it emits to space. How does this relate to the first law of thermodynamics?
options: Energy is created by the oceans and core, so Earth emits more energy than it receives from the Sun
Energy cannot leave Earth, so all solar energy received is stored permanently in the oceans
Energy entering must be stored, transformed or leave, so steady temperature needs input to equal output
Energy entering the system is destroyed in the atmosphere, so Earth never warms whatever the input
questions.explanation: Because energy is conserved, any difference between incoming and outgoing energy must change the amount stored in the Earth system, raising or lowering temperatures. When input and output are equal, the stored energy and average temperature stay steady.

questions.stem: Sunlight strikes a eucalypt leaf. Which statement correctly applies the first law of thermodynamics?
options: The light energy is converted to chemical energy, heat and reflected light, with the total unchanged
The light energy is destroyed inside the leaf, so less energy leaves than arrived at the leaf
The light energy is multiplied by photosynthesis, so the leaf stores more energy than it received
The light energy is converted entirely into chemical energy, with none lost as heat or reflected
questions.explanation: Some of the light is reflected, some is converted to chemical energy in sugars and some becomes heat, but the total equals the energy that arrived. No transformation is perfectly efficient, and energy is never destroyed or multiplied.

questions.stem: Which mode of energy transfer carries energy from the Sun to Earth through the vacuum of space?
options: Conduction
Convection
Advection
Radiation
questions.explanation: Radiation is the transfer of energy by electromagnetic waves, which need no medium, so it is the only way energy crosses space. Conduction and convection need matter to carry the energy.

questions.stem: Conduction is the transfer of thermal energy:
options: By electromagnetic waves that can travel through empty space
By the evaporation and condensation of water vapour in the air
Through direct contact between particles, without the material itself moving
By the bulk movement of a heated fluid from one place to another
questions.explanation: In conduction, vibrating particles pass energy to neighbouring particles, so heat moves through a material without the material flowing. It is most important in solids such as rock. Bulk movement of fluid is convection.

questions.stem: Which example from Earth systems is mainly convection?
options: Warm air rising above a sun-heated paddock and cooler air sinking nearby
Heat moving upward through the solid rock of the continental crust
Sunlight warming the surface of the ocean on a cloudless summer day
A hot rock warming the sand directly beneath it on a beach at noon
questions.explanation: Convection is energy transfer by the movement of a heated fluid: warm, less dense air rises and cooler, denser air sinks. Heat moving through solid crust and from hot rock to sand is conduction, and sunlight reaching the ocean is radiation.

questions.stem: Why is conduction the main way heat moves through Earth's rigid lithosphere, while convection dominates in the mantle below?
options: The lithosphere is a vacuum, so only conduction can occur, while the mantle contains moving water
The lithosphere is cold and rigid, so it cannot flow, while hot mantle rock flows slowly over long periods
The lithosphere is liquid, so heat moves by currents, while the mantle is a gas that conducts heat
The lithosphere receives heat only by radiation from space, while the mantle receives it from the Sun
questions.explanation: Convection requires material that can flow. Hot mantle rock, though solid, flows very slowly over millions of years and carries heat by convection. The cooler lithosphere behaves rigidly, so heat crosses it mainly by conduction.

questions.stem: A student heats one side of a beaker of oil containing tea leaves. The leaves rise above the heat, move across the top, sink at the far side and return along the bottom. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Heat travels by conduction through the leaves, which move because they are warmer than the oil
Heated fluid becomes less dense and rises, setting up a convection current that carries energy
Heat travels through the oil by radiation, which pushes the tea leaves away from the flame
Heated fluid becomes more dense and rises, while cooler fluid becomes less dense and sinks
questions.explanation: Oil near the heat expands, becomes less dense and rises, while cooler, denser oil sinks to replace it, forming a loop that carries energy. This models convection in the mantle, atmosphere and oceans. Warmer fluid is less dense, not more.

questions.stem: Temperature measured in a deep mine increases from 20 °C at the surface to 70 °C at 2 km depth. What is the average geothermal gradient?
options: 45 °C per km
25 °C per km
35 °C per km
50 °C per km
questions.explanation: The temperature rises by 70 − 20 = 50 °C over 2 km, so the gradient is 50 ÷ 2 = 25 °C per km. Dividing 70 °C by 2 km, or forgetting to divide by the depth, gives the wrong values.

questions.stem: A graph shows the surface temperature of dry sand and of a nearby water-filled tray under the same sunlight. The sand warms faster during the day and cools faster at night. What does this data show?
options: Water needs more energy than sand to change temperature, so it stores heat and changes temperature slowly
Sand absorbs no radiation, so its temperature changes only because of conduction from the air
Water reflects nearly all of the sunlight, so it never stores any energy during the day
Sand and water store the same energy, but the thermometer in the sand gives higher readings
questions.explanation: Water has a much higher specific heat capacity than sand, so the same energy input raises its temperature less, and it releases stored heat slowly at night. This is why oceans act as heat sinks and moderate coastal climates.

questions.stem: Which process transforms light energy into chemical energy stored in Earth's biosphere?
options: Respiration
Convection
Photosynthesis
Evaporation
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose and other organic molecules. Respiration releases that stored energy, evaporation stores energy as latent heat in water vapour, and convection transfers heat.

questions.stem: When water evaporates from the ocean surface, where is the absorbed energy stored?
options: As chemical energy in the salt left behind in the ocean when water evaporates
As light energy in the water vapour, which glows when clouds begin to form
As gravitational energy in the ocean floor, which rises as water is lost
As latent heat in the water vapour, which is released when the vapour condenses
questions.explanation: Evaporation absorbs energy, which is held as latent heat in the vapour without raising its temperature. When the vapour condenses into cloud droplets, this energy is released, warming the surrounding air.

questions.stem: The oceans are described as a heat sink in the Earth system. What does this mean?
options: They produce heat from chemical reactions and release it into the atmosphere
They reflect most incoming solar energy back into space without absorbing it
They lose heat to the core, which removes energy from the Earth system
They absorb and store large amounts of thermal energy, releasing it slowly
questions.explanation: Because water has a high heat capacity and the oceans are vast and deep, they absorb and store enormous amounts of energy, releasing it slowly. Oceans have absorbed most of the extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases in recent decades.

questions.stem: Which energy transformation occurs as a tectonic plate moves?
options: Light energy from the Sun is transformed into kinetic energy of the plates
Thermal energy from the interior is transformed into kinetic energy of moving rock
Kinetic energy of moving rock is transformed into light energy from the Sun
Chemical energy in the crust is transformed into electrical energy in the core
questions.explanation: Heat from Earth's interior drives mantle convection and makes material buoyant or dense, producing movement, so thermal energy (and gravitational potential energy) becomes kinetic energy. Plate motion is driven from within, not by sunlight.

questions.stem: Which phase change in the water cycle releases energy to the surroundings?
options: Evaporation of water from the surface of a lake
Melting of snow on a mountain in spring
Sublimation of ice directly into water vapour
Condensation of water vapour into cloud droplets
questions.explanation: Condensation releases the latent heat that was absorbed during evaporation, warming the surrounding air. Evaporation, melting and sublimation all absorb energy.

questions.stem: Tropical cyclones in the Coral Sea gain much of their energy from warm ocean water. Which process supplies this energy?
options: Absorption of latent heat as rain droplets freeze into hail inside the storm clouds
Conduction of heat from the sea floor through the ocean water into the storm
Radiation of heat from the storm clouds down onto the surface of the ocean
Release of latent heat as water vapour from the warm ocean condenses in the storm clouds
questions.explanation: Warm seas supply abundant water vapour. When it rises and condenses, the latent heat released warms the air, making it rise faster and strengthening the storm. Freezing also releases heat, but condensation is the main source.

questions.stem: Which source supplies the energy that evaporates water and drives the water cycle?
options: Solar radiation absorbed at Earth's surface
Heat conducted from Earth's core to the ocean floor
Kinetic energy of rivers flowing down to the sea
Chemical energy released by photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Thermal and light energy from the Sun heat the surface and evaporate water, lifting it into the atmosphere. Gravity then returns it as precipitation and runoff. Geothermal heat is tiny compared with solar input.

questions.stem: Rain falls on a high plateau and flows down through a hydro-electric station. Which sequence of energy transformations is correct, starting from the Sun?
options: Solar energy is converted directly into kinetic energy of the river, without any change in potential energy
Solar energy evaporates and lifts water; the rain's gravitational potential energy becomes kinetic energy as it flows
Solar energy heats the rock; the rock warms the rain, giving it chemical energy that becomes gravitational energy as it flows
Solar energy is stored in clouds as kinetic energy; the rain then converts this to latent heat as it flows downhill
questions.explanation: Solar energy evaporates water, and rising vapour that condenses at height leaves water with gravitational potential energy. As the water flows downhill this becomes kinetic energy, which turbines convert to electrical energy.

questions.stem: On a hot day, a person feels cooler after a swim as the water evaporates from their skin. How does this relate to the water cycle?
options: Evaporation stores energy in the skin, the same process that forms ice sheets at the poles
Evaporation creates new energy in the air, the same process that drives mantle convection
Evaporation absorbs energy from surfaces, the same process that transfers energy from oceans to the air
Evaporation releases energy into the skin, the same process that warms the oceans each summer
questions.explanation: Evaporation takes latent heat from the surface it leaves, cooling it. On a global scale, evaporation from oceans and plants transfers huge amounts of energy into the atmosphere, released later when clouds form.

questions.stem: What is a major source of the heat inside Earth?
options: Sunlight conducted down through the crust over millions of years
Friction from ocean tides rubbing against the sea floor
Decay of radioactive isotopes such as uranium, thorium and potassium-40
Chemical reactions between oxygen and iron in the outer core
questions.explanation: Radioactive decay of long-lived isotopes such as uranium-238, thorium-232 and potassium-40 releases heat continuously, together with heat left over from Earth's formation. Sunlight warms only the top few metres of the ground.

questions.stem: How is heat transferred from Earth's core to its surface?
options: By convection in the crust, then by radiation from the mantle to the core
Into the mantle, up by mantle convection, then by conduction through the lithosphere
By radiation directly from the core through the mantle and crust to the surface
By conduction alone through a liquid mantle and crust, taking only a few days
questions.explanation: Heat leaves the core into the base of the mantle, mantle convection carries it upward over millions of years, and it then conducts through the rigid lithosphere to the surface, escaping fastest at volcanoes and mid-ocean ridges.

questions.stem: Why does Earth's interior remain hot after about 4.5 billion years, when a small rock would have cooled long ago?
options: The core is made of ice that releases heat as it slowly melts under pressure
Heat cannot escape from Earth because the crust is a perfect insulator
Radioactive decay keeps adding heat, and a huge body of rock loses heat slowly
The Sun continually reheats the core through the oceans and the crust
questions.explanation: Heat from radioactive decay is continually added, and Earth's great size means its interior loses heat very slowly. Heat does escape, as volcanoes and the geothermal gradient show, so the crust is not a perfect insulator.

questions.stem: Geothermal power stations generate electricity using heat from Earth's interior. Why is geothermal energy described as a low carbon emission source?
options: It uses heat from the ground instead of burning fuel, so it emits little carbon dioxide
It removes carbon dioxide from the air and stores it as rock in the hot crust
It burns coal deep underground, so the carbon dioxide stays trapped in the rock
It runs on sunlight absorbed by the crust, so it produces no waste or emissions of any kind
questions.explanation: Geothermal plants use hot water or steam heated by Earth's internal heat, so no fuel is burnt and carbon dioxide emissions are low. Small amounts of gas can be released from geothermal fluids, but far less than from fossil fuels.

questions.stem: What is slab pull?
options: The pull of the Moon's gravity on the crust, which moves plates each month
A cold, dense subducting plate sinking under gravity and pulling the rest of the plate
The push of hot magma rising at a mid-ocean ridge, which forces two plates apart
The drag of strong winds on the ocean surface, which moves the plate below it
questions.explanation: Old oceanic lithosphere is cold and dense, so where it subducts it sinks into the mantle under gravity and pulls the attached plate behind it. Slab pull is thought to be one of the strongest forces driving plate motion.

questions.stem: Which energy transformation takes place in slab pull?
options: Kinetic energy becomes chemical energy as the slab reacts with the mantle
Light energy becomes thermal energy as sunlight warms the subducting slab
Thermal energy becomes light energy as the slab glows in the deep mantle
Gravitational potential energy becomes kinetic energy as the dense slab sinks
questions.explanation: As the dense slab sinks, it loses gravitational potential energy, which becomes kinetic energy of moving rock, and some is converted to heat by friction. Sunlight plays no part in driving subduction.

questions.stem: How do mantle convection currents help move tectonic plates?
options: Hot mantle rises, spreads beneath the lithosphere and cools and sinks, and plates move with this circulation
Cold mantle rises, warms at the surface and sinks again, pushing plates towards the hottest regions
Liquid mantle flows rapidly in rivers under the crust, carrying plates several metres a year
The mantle stays still, but plates float freely on liquid outer core and drift with Earth's spin
questions.explanation: Heat from below makes mantle rock less dense so it rises, while cooler, denser rock sinks. This slow circulation, together with slab pull, is linked to plate motion of a few centimetres a year. The mantle is solid but flows slowly; the plates are not floating on the outer core.

questions.stem: A mantle plume is best described as:
options: A column of unusually hot mantle rock rising from deep within Earth
A cold slab of oceanic crust sinking into the mantle at a trench
A cloud of ash and gas rising from an erupting volcano into the air
A layer of liquid iron surrounding the solid inner core
questions.explanation: A mantle plume is a narrow upwelling of hot, buoyant mantle rock. Where it reaches the base of the lithosphere it can melt rock and produce hotspot volcanoes. A sinking slab is the opposite, cold downward movement.

questions.stem: The Hawaiian Islands form a chain in which the volcanoes get older with distance north-west of the active island of Hawaii. Which explanation fits the evidence?
options: The plume moves south-east beneath a stationary Pacific Plate, building a new volcano every few years
Slab pull drags the islands towards the plume, so the oldest volcanoes are always closest to it
Each volcano formed from a separate plume at the same time, and erosion makes some look older
The plate moves over a fixed plume, carrying each volcano away as a new one forms above it
questions.explanation: A hotspot track forms when a plate moves over a relatively fixed plume. The active volcano sits over the plume, and older, extinct volcanoes lie in the direction the plate has carried them. Radiometric dates of the islands confirm their age sequence.

questions.stem: Which statement best compares the roles of mantle convection and slab pull in moving plates?
options: Both involve gravity acting on temperature-driven density differences; slab pull acts on the plate itself
Mantle convection is driven by sunlight, while slab pull is driven by tides, so they are unrelated
Slab pull happens only at mid-ocean ridges, while convection happens only at subduction zones
Mantle convection moves plates in a few days, while slab pull takes millions of years
questions.explanation: Both result from heat making rock less dense where it is hot and denser where it is cold, with gravity driving the motion. In slab pull, the cold, dense plate itself is the sinking part of the circulation. Slab pull acts at subduction zones, not ridges.

questions.stem: In which year did Alfred Wegener first propose his theory of continental drift in a lecture?
questions.explanation: Wegener presented the idea of continental drift in a lecture in Frankfurt in 1912 and published an expanded version in his book The Origin of Continents and Oceans in 1915. Sea-floor evidence supporting plate tectonics came decades later.

questions.stem: Which evidence did Wegener use to support continental drift?
options: Measurements of plate speeds made with satellites and global positioning systems
Magnetic stripes on the sea floor recorded on either side of mid-ocean ridges
Seismic shadow zones recorded by stations around the world after earthquakes
Matching coastlines, fossils such as Glossopteris, and rocks on separate continents
questions.explanation: Wegener pointed to the fit of continents such as South America and Africa, the same fossils and rock types on widely separated continents, and evidence of past glaciation. Satellite measurements and sea-floor magnetic stripes came much later.

questions.stem: Why was Wegener's theory of continental drift rejected by most geologists for decades after 1915?
options: He could not give a convincing mechanism to explain how the continents moved
His fossil evidence was shown to be faked by other scientists of the time
Continents were known to be fixed because satellite data showed no movement
He claimed the continents moved several kilometres each year, which was disproved
questions.explanation: Critics argued that Wegener's proposed forces were far too weak to move continents. Acceptance came only when sea-floor spreading and mantle convection provided a mechanism. Satellite data did not exist until much later.

questions.stem: How did Wegener's continental drift theory change to become the modern theory of plate tectonics?
options: Wegener's evidence was discarded, and plate tectonics was based only on new computer models
Geologists found that continents move through the oceanic crust, as Wegener had described
The theory was accepted unchanged once more scientists agreed with Wegener's ideas
Evidence from the sea floor showed new crust forming and plates moving, supplying the missing mechanism
questions.explanation: Discoveries such as sea-floor spreading, magnetic striping and the distribution of earthquakes showed that whole lithospheric plates move, driven by mantle processes. Wegener's matching fossils and rocks were retained as evidence, but continents do not plough through oceanic crust.

questions.stem: Heat flow measured through the sea floor is much higher at a mid-ocean ridge than across the old interior of a continent. What best explains this data?
options: Hot mantle rock rises close to the surface at ridges, so heat has only a thin layer to cross
Sea water at ridges is warmed by the Sun more strongly than the land in continental interiors
Continental interiors contain no radioactive isotopes, so they produce no heat of their own
Ridges are made of thick, cold crust that stores heat and then releases it all at once
questions.explanation: At mid-ocean ridges hot mantle upwells and the new lithosphere is thin and young, so heat reaches the surface quickly. Old continental interiors have thick, cold lithosphere through which heat must conduct slowly. Continental crust actually contains relatively high concentrations of radioactive isotopes.

questions.stem: Coal formed from plants that grew in swamps hundreds of millions of years ago. Which statement correctly describes the energy stored in coal?
options: It is kinetic energy from the rivers that carried the plant material into the swamps
It is nuclear energy released when the plant material decayed inside the swamp water
It is solar energy transformed by photosynthesis and stored as chemical energy for a very long time
It is geothermal energy absorbed by the coal from Earth's core while the coal was buried
questions.explanation: Plants converted light energy into chemical energy by photosynthesis, and burial preserved some of that organic matter as coal. Burning coal releases this stored ancient solar energy. Heat from burial helps turn plant matter into coal, but the stored energy came from sunlight.

questions.stem: Which mode of energy transfer depends on a fluid that can flow?
options: Radiation
Reflection
Convection
Conduction
questions.explanation: Convection carries energy by the bulk movement of a fluid such as air, water or slowly flowing mantle rock. Conduction can occur in solids without flow, and radiation needs no medium at all.
